Мысли выходного дня. Достаточно давно пришел к мнению, что современный tech очень другой по сравнению с тем, что было ранее. Давайте поясню. 
Большая часть рынка и людей сейчас в tech живут прошлым. Огого можно сделать себе дашборд, софтик для трекинга калорий или планер. Иногда эти мечты выходят за пределы личного софта и начинается игра как раньше. Мол я сделаю людям же надо. Но кажется время ушло. 
Мне нравится следующая аналогия. В середине прошлой декады появились хорошие камеры в телефонах чтобы снимать видосы, эффекты всякие и прочее. Это сделало возможным каждому снять норм ролик, ведь теперь видеокамера не нужна. Абсолютно каждый «сам себе режиссер». Вот тоже самое будет с софтом. Надо становится блогером. Быть личностью. Уметь привлекать людей к себе. А это прошлое поколение предпринимателей совсем не умеет. 
Все акселераторы, венчура и прочая туса заточена оценивать продукт, трек рекорды и прочее. Но как мы знаем это то, что блогеру совсем не обязательно нужно. И рост который тоже все оценивали теперь надо оценивать иначе. Теперь каждый под запуском из YC пишет как он повторил весь продукт через один промт. И вот это ровно тот же эффект как у блогеров. Выложить похожий ролик проще простого. Но залетают едицницы. 
Велкам ту экономика внимания вместо экономика продукта и роста. 
А серьезный софт останется там же. Это модели, рисерч, интеграция, железо и прочее. Где порог входа вырастет в сотни раз. Такие дела.
posts.text_en:
Weekend thoughts. Quite a while ago I came to the opinion that modern tech is very different compared to what it used to be. Let me explain.

Most of the market and people in tech right now live in the past. Wow, you can make yourself a dashboard, some little calorie-tracking software, or a planner. Sometimes these dreams go beyond personal software and the “like it used to be” game starts. Like, I’ll make it, people need it. But it seems that time is gone.

I like the following analogy. In the middle of the last decade, good cameras showed up in phones so you could shoot vids, all sorts of effects and whatever. That made it possible for anyone to shoot a decent clip, because now you don’t need a video camera. Absolutely everyone is “their own director.” The exact same thing is gonna happen with software. You’ve gotta become a blogger. Be a persona. Know how to pull people toward you. And the previous generation of entrepreneurs absolutely can’t do that.

All the accelerators, VC, and the whole тусa are tuned to evaluate product, track records, and whatever. But as we know, that’s not something a blogger necessarily needs at all. And “growth,” which everyone used to evaluate too, now has to be evaluated differently. Now every other person under a YC launch writes about how they replicated the whole product with one prompt. And that’s exactly the same effect as with bloggers. Posting a similar video is easy as hell. But only a few go viral.

Welcome to the attention economy instead of the product-and-growth economy.

And serious software will stay right where it is. Models, research, integration, hardware, and so on. Where the barrier to entry will grow by hundreds of times. That’s how it is.

Накопилось много всякого, что хотелось бы написать. Там и s1 Anthropic и разные другие кризисы кредитования compute бизнеса. Но начну пожалуй с математики. 
Ремарка: я не ученый и тем более не математик. Но пол жизни провел в математике и достаточно плотно интересовался ей, даже в институт Стеклова при РАН ходил. Ну кто знает, тот поймет. 
Так вот OpenAI накинули очень сильный 
результат (https://openai.com/index/building-scientific-understanding-with-academic-communities/)
 на прошлой неделе. Это не какие-то там мелочи. Это что-то около премии Филдса (аналог нобелевки но в математике). Очень крутые вещи. Правда предстоит еще ревью. Но тем не менее. 
Так вот я считаю что настало очень важное время в математических дисциплинах. Двигаться в некоторых доменах стало легко и осталось понять куда. Я думаю что большая часть математики была настолько далека от прикладной части, что развивалась как теория без понятного ракурса как ее применить. Думаю, что в таких местах AI поможет ой как хорошо. Ученому лишь надо задать вектор и оно само найдет, соединит и докажет. Доказательство ради доказательств начнет исчезать, а это был большой пласт математики. 
Но мне думается, самый сок не в таких областях. А в той самой теор физике или областях на стыках нескольких наук или направлений. Самое интересное где AI найдет что-то чего человек в силу величины области просто не мог подобрать и соотнести. Сколько всего можно нового узнать. И тут без «human in the loop» думаю пока никуда. Все-таки с сооружением новых концептов без указки оно пока не едет. Но перебором владеет мастерски. 
Поэтому в науку идти станет интереснее. И исчезнут всякие сугубо теор в три уровня подвижки. Ибо намного важнее будет уметь соединять это с экспериментом и реальностью. 
Но время покажет.
posts.text_en:
A lot of stuff has piled up that I’d like to write about. There’s s1 Anthropic in there, and various other lending crises of the compute business. But I’ll start, I guess, with math.  
Note: I’m not a scientist and even less a mathematician. But I spent half my life in math and was pretty deeply into it, I even used to go to the Steklov Institute at the Russian Academy of Sciences. Well, those who know, will get it.  

So. OpenAI dropped a seriously strong result last week. This isn’t some little trifles. This is something on the order of a Fields Medal (the Nobel analogue but for math). Very cool stuff. Sure, it still has to go through review. But still.  

So I think a very important time has come in mathematical disciplines. Moving in certain domains has become easy, and what’s left is to understand where to move. I think a big chunk of math was so far removed from the applied part that it developed as theory with no clear angle on how to use it. I think in places like that AI will help like hell. The scientist just needs to set the vector and it’ll find it, connect it, and prove it. Proof for the sake of proofs will start to vanish, and that was a huge layer of math.  

But I think the real juice isn’t in those areas. It’s in that very theoretical physics, or in areas at the junction of several sciences or directions. The most interesting thing is where AI will find something a human, due to the sheer size of the field, simply couldn’t pick out and line up. How much new stuff you can learn. And here, without “human in the loop,” I think there’s still no getting around it for now. It still doesn’t really go, building new concepts without being pointed. But it does brute force like a master.  

So it’ll become more interesting to go into science. And all sorts of purely-theoretical, three-level nudges will disappear. Because it’ll be way more important to be able to connect it to experiment and reality.  

But time will tell.

Links:
https://openai.com/index/building-scientific-understanding-with-academic-communities/

Всем особо обеспокоенным напоминаю несколько деталей последних событий:
1/ взлом HuggingFace агентами это блин не «модель такая сидит и думает как бы ей сломать какой-то сервис». Это конкретный набор инструкций из exploitgym который напрямую указывал что делать. Ничего сами агенты пока не ломают (по собственной инициативе). Что за чушь?
2/ ai решает сам задачу тысячелетия! Все нам конец. Нет. Не сам он решил. Взяли ребята огромный пласт готового рисерча и обучались на трейсах и дальше по-умному забрутфорсили (так же как с другими гипотезами). Самостоятельно никакая модель пока ничего не решает. Попробуй сам. 
3/ но самое 
забавно (https://x.com/parkerthayer/status/2097759699626328575?s=46)
 это пост какого-то там чела 27 летнего который поработал в OpenAI и потом в антропике начал качать тему: аи нас всех убьет. Вас скорее убьет что-то типа машины на дорого чем аи. Если в целом кого-то беспокоят такие риски советую не выходить из дома уже сейчас.
posts.text_en:
To everyone especially freaking out, I’ll remind you of a few details about the latest events:
1/ the HuggingFace “hack” by agents is, damn, not “some model sitting there thinking how it could break some service.” It was a very specific set of instructions from exploitgym that directly told it what to do. Agents themselves aren’t breaking anything yet (on their own initiative). What is this nonsense?
2/ AI solves a millennium-old problem all by itself! That’s it, we’re all done for. No. It didn’t solve it by itself. Some guys took a massive chunk of existing research and trained on traces and then brute-forced it intelligently (same as with other hypotheses). No model is solving anything on its own yet. Try it yourself.
3/ but the funniest part
is this post by some 27-year-old dude who worked at OpenAI and then at Anthropic and started pushing this line: AI will kill us all. You’re more likely to get killed by something like a car on the road than by AI. If these risks bother you in general, I recommend not leaving your house starting now.

- pure research, yeah, because even if you don’t really do jack shit, they’ll buy you as a team. The whole point is to assemble a solid lineup. The rest isn’t that important. Betting on neo-labs at funds is popular. Because the money returns are almost guaranteed.
- application layer. But here it’s important to understand what’s relevant is more the UX part, not the business part. Labs and big companies have a need to implement certain features (look at OpenAI’s acquisitions)
Pretty much all of this is hard to validate without deep domain knowledge. Absolutely not relevant outside certain geographies and without talent onboard. That’s how it is.

Короче rage bait пост. Про бизнес, предпринимателей, венчур и «взрослую индустрию tech». 
TLDR: венчуру в его текущем виде конец, будут только большие раунды, предприниматели прошлого цикла (а-ля инстаграм кофаундеры) потеряли свою ценность, их опыт не нужен. 
А теперь по порядку. Мы находимся у порога технологического цикла. Входного порога конечно. AI такая штука которая срезает все «среднее», «ну такое» и прочее ниже этого по качеству. Технология меняет местами в приоритете две важных вещи. Возможность сделать и возможность проверить. 
Раньше самым большим порогом входа было: собрать команду, найти денег чтобы им платить, мотивировать и так далее. Поток людей в индустрию рос. Было много гипотез, но чтобы их проверить нужно было время и ресурсы. Гипотезы были очень простые. О давай продавать это или отмечать фотки на карте, отмечать клиентов в табличке и трекать прогресс. Все было открыто (интернет меньше регулировался). Поэтому предприниматели славились своими софт скилами. Не так важно было знать проблему и ее решать, важно было найти людей и итерировать. Это ценилось превыше всего. 
Сегодня я вижу картинку по-другому. Порог до проверки гипотезы упал до нельзя. Простые вещи проверить можно на коленке. Посмотрите на вайбкодинг подделки. И тут оказалось, что решение проблемы в RL стоит сотни миллионов, а твой новый SaaS две выручки дай бог. И для меня поменялось местами следующее. Раньше важно найти с кем и засетапить. Теперь важно очень точно понимать что делать, и желательно формулировать конкретно. И это пресловутое знание в век AI компаний оказалось очень техническим и очень сложным. Залетели первые компании типа perplexity & Harvey. А дальше читая описание компаний поднимающих 200м сразу даже не понятно. И это не потому что они делают чушь (клоуны ахахах), а потому что не понимаешь в чем вообще суть проблемы ими решаемой. 
Следом за кризисом у предпринимателей будет кризис аллокации капитала. Ведь теперь нужно разбираться «на что» давать бабки, а не кому давать бабки. Что очень ломает мир инвесторов. И софт скилы отходят на второй план, ведь собрать команду под четкую проблему и зная что внутри легче, чем под «Тиндер для собак». А значит нужны инвесторы которые шарят. А таких будет мало, ибо им легче сделать свою компанию. 
Все эти вещи можно заметить уже сейчас: топ рисерч челы уходят из гугла, в инвест фондах меняются лица, потому что прошлые лидеры просто не понимают что происходит. Тупо банально не вдупляют в смысл происходящего. 
Такая стадия во многих индустриях. Там где венчура то и нет. Где стало сильно меньше высокорисковых идей с потенциалом. Потому что идеи стали сложные слишком. Это нас ждет и в tech. И да я бы не инвестировал бабки в трек рекорд прошлых лет, а лучше бы студентам норм профессора по ml закинул. Такие дела. 
Вторую часть может тоже напишу. Но предрекаю огромное количество «великих предпринимателей» у которыхт в эпоху AI ничего не выйдет. Совсем.
posts.text_en:
In short, a rage bait post. About business, entrepreneurs, venture, and the “grown-up tech industry.”
TLDR: venture as it exists now is over, there’ll only be big rounds, entrepreneurs from the previous cycle (like Instagram cofounders) have lost their value, their experience isn’t needed.

Now in order. We’re standing at the threshold of a tech cycle. The entry threshold, obviously. AI is the kind of thing that cuts off all the “mid,” the “eh, kinda,” and everything below that in quality. The tech swaps two important things in priority: the ability to make and the ability to verify.

Before, the biggest entry barrier was: assemble a team, find money to pay them, motivate them, etc. The flow of people into the industry was growing. There were tons of hypotheses, but to test them you needed time and resources. The hypotheses were super simple. Like oh let’s sell this, or tag photos on a map, tag clients in a spreadsheet and track progress. Everything was open (the internet was less regulated). That’s why entrepreneurs were famous for their soft skills. It wasn’t that important to know the problem and solve it, it was important to find people and iterate. That was valued above all.

Today I see the picture differently. The barrier to testing a hypothesis has dropped to basically nothing. Simple things you can test on your knee. Look at the vibe-coding knockoffs. And then it turned out that solving the problem in the real world costs hundreds of millions, while your new SaaS is, God willing, two revenues. And for me the following flipped. Before it was important to find who with and set it up. Now it’s important to understand very precisely what to do, and ideally to formulate it concretely. And that notorious “knowledge” in the age of AI companies turned out to be very technical and very hard.

The first companies like Perplexity & Harvey made it in. And then reading the descriptions of companies raising 200m right away, it’s not even clear. And it’s not because they’re making bullshit (clowns lolol), it’s because you don’t understand what the essence of the problem they’re solving even is.

After the crisis among entrepreneurs there will be a capital allocation crisis. Because now you need to understand “what” to give money to, not who to give money to. Which really breaks the investors’ world. And soft skills move to the background, because assembling a team for a clear problem and knowing what’s inside is easier than for “Tinder for dogs.” Which means you need investors who actually get it. And there will be few of those, because it’s easier for them to build their own company.

You can already see all this now: top research people are leaving Google, faces in investment funds are changing, because the previous leaders just don’t understand what’s happening. Just straight up, basically, don’t grok the meaning of what’s going on.

This stage exists in a lot of industries. Where there basically isn’t venture. Where there have become way fewer high-risk ideas with potential. Because the ideas got too complex. That’s what’s coming for us in tech too. And yeah, I wouldn’t invest money in a track record from past years, I’d rather throw it at students and good ML professors. That’s how it is.

Maybe I’ll write a second part too. But I’m predicting a huge number of “great entrepreneurs” who, in the AI era, won’t get anything to work. At all.

Observations from the last few weeks.  
1/ there are two camps on how to reach AGI — we’ve got rsi (recursive self improvement) and world models. The first is represented by Anthropic & OpenAI. The second by Google DeepMind. And because the DeepMind leader doesn’t believe OpenAI is pulling it off, you supposedly need to do both, and that’s why everything is so slow. Basically a corporate delay. But whose bet will hit is unclear to literally anyone.  
2/ people are returning to China — the ones working at top places in the US. Main idea: they believe they’ll be able, like the US back in the day, to pull off the “Chinese dream,” namely get valuation multiples for their companies that are several times higher. In other words we’re in for Chinese dominance in AI. I’d say that’s more than likely. Given the amount of effort and faith. And super talents.  
3/ a crisis is brewing in math. Many PhDs are, to put it mildly, going to get devalued. And I think there’ll be a big restructuring of the whole science world in general. Because AI will be able to literally discover and solve 50% of current problems. And there still aren’t any “totally new” meanings in sight. And I think the problem of finding something new is the same as the problem of writing text that resonates. Because in relativity theory what matters is not so much the theory as the idea. After that you can, so to speak, run the rest of the way somehow.  
4/ hiring is hell. A regular researcher at Anthropic (and other top labs) gets 10m+ over 4 years. Life is pain.  
5/ a lot of companies have barely realized that scaling depends on their ability to train their own models. Harvey, Cursor (couldn’t and gave up to do it somewhere else) and others

A few observations. About “job hunting.” I regularly stumble on Russian-language posts like “I’m awesome, but yeah, such is life, looking for a job.” I’ll try to toss in my two cents from the hiring side:

- if someone is sooo awesome, like insanely wow, and the comments are all these metaphors like “you’re wow,” then why the hell are you, sorry, looking for a job? There have to be reasons, and if there are uncontrollable circumstances, that’s exactly where I’d start
- all these weird, purely-ours sayings: my superpower, what I do best is see “profit/systemness/collect meanings and turn them into releases AND so on” — what is that even about? Never understood all these abstract descriptions. Imagine a footballer telling his agent “I see the team’s philosophy and I can figure out how to steel my resolve and play.” Well damn, everyone’s like that. Give me something I can actually touch
- the first thing I’ll do is go grab references, if the role is above line-level, and the description is exactly about that, and then I don’t give a crap about all your “searching for meaning and ability to assemble systems”
- life happens in different ways, sure, but you still need to bring your awesomeness into something measurable — either via references or via metrics
- please cut out your vibe-coding craft projects, they show your total lack of understanding of the market more often than the opposite

And I’ve never once seen posts on the US market, where supposedly the competition is tougher, in the style of “I’m super awesome, but give me money, I’m looking for a job.” In my head those two things just don’t fit together very well. And probably that’s why they don’t do it here. Edited: for roles above line-level.

My recommendations, after looking through a ton of resumes and reading posts and actually searching for people for my team:

- write honestly what you did and what you got done, don’t decorate it, if your position isn’t line-level
- focus, obviously, on what matters in the application
- remove all the superpowers, whining, life situation, and the long story — it kills any desire to talk (we’re strangers, after all)
- showing desire matters most
- specify who can recommend you

I’ll toss something into the stash about frontier labs. Online people love to yap about Open Weight Models. Like they’re about to catch up any minute now and are always breathing down their necks. What I think after talking to different folks, and what problems I see:

• the talent problem: how do you hire a team to build a small or open model if a solid research talent at Anthropic is pulling $10M a year (real numbers), and you still need compute and all that stuff  
• say you’re ready to invest in training people for a year or two, but then you’ll be catching up forever — how do you solve that? well you need to raise a hundred mil or two right away and chill, otherwise I don’t really get what the competitive advantage in the offer is  
• but say you do lure people with upside, then there’s this opinion going around that “frontier models are 90% of the market in money”, where do you get data for training and RL from, i.e. literally everyone only buys “the best” (they’re ready to pay a market premium for “a model that’s a bit better” — pay 20% more or even 2x)  
• a условный Opus is 10x more expensive than Chinese models and everyone buys it  
• in this situation competition gets even harder because they start covering up the distillation process with the fact that there are closed models for industries and even special deploy teams that integrate those models in closed mode (see Mythos, and OpenAI’s math models). Or in other words: distilling a model into Claude Code will be easy, but the one that runs in a bank — no way.

All this looks like a typical oligopoly and I think there won’t be room for OSS over time except for certain verticals or solutions. I think the Chinese make everything open just to have at least some data and attract people. I don’t see any other real reasons.

Oh and decentralized inference is bullshit.

posts.text_en:
A thought crept in. Doesn’t it seem to you that a harness is technical debt, since there are systems there that rely on specific prompts. Like, in practice we’re hoping that a phrase worded in a certain way will give a better result. But that changes with every model version.

So even if the model changed (even if they suddenly slipped a quantized one into your API or switched the inference version) everything can drift apart on you? Turns out prompts—and the more of them you have—are a kind of technical debt, and a hefty one at that. Maintaining something you don’t understand is a so-so task. In the sense that without knowing what the model does well and what data they poured in, making prompts is gonna be rough.

Overall my take: if the model was trained properly on certain tasks, the prompt’s influence won’t be that big. But on the other hand Cloudflare reports after experiments on Mythos that, like, harness is our everything. Where the truth is isn’t clear, but what’s definitely clear to me is: building “forever” harnesses without your own model is shooting yourself in the foot.

Observations.
Every week I get about 20 projects/products/teams coming in and telling me what they did/plan to do and so on. What I usually notice:
1/ Decks, all the materials, blurbs, emails are made through AI. You can straight up see that people didn’t read what they themselves made, decks are a hundred-fucking pages, vibe-coded frontends—you know, with that Claude Design aftertaste (that’s when you ask it to make it pretty please). And they all expect that someone will dig into this and study it and, what’s more, give them money?
2/ Most projects don’t know evals even exist. An agent to “plug in some thing” or we’ll improve your agent for “some thing.” But how to understand that the proposed approach is better than the basic “just feed everything to ChatGPT,” no clue. At least go look at benchmarks and scoring systems or something.
3/ Well even if there are zero evals and benches, then you should be paying for that. Otherwise it’s really hard to understand what to do and how to evaluate any of it.
4/ A ton of “slop,” meaning I spend 2–3 minutes and see factual/numerical errors in the materials. Like they write market size and two numbers multiplied give the wrong result. And there’s just a ton of that. No desire to read and talk to a person who didn’t even check what they wrote.
5/ Everyone asks for millions, and I don’t understand why. Everything that was done was done with a $200/month subscription. Why do you need millions?
6/ People don’t know the basics. Yeah yeah, the difference between a harness and a model, what metrics mean what, don’t know about recall etc. in search tasks. What is there even to talk about then?
It adds up to a strong feeling that they don’t even write the texts and answers to questions themselves. And that’s sad, and that’s exactly why it’s gotten harder to do anything if you don’t think for yourself, but if you’ve got your own head on your shoulders then now is the best time, of course!

If you saw somewhere some info, clickbait, an interview about how to make your first cash in venture. With a project or an idea. Then please check these three points and don’t listen to air stirrers.

They’ll give you money for your idea or team or product if:
1/ you have a track record, meaning previous results that are known in the industry
2/ you have metrics (measurable traction) at the moment you’re raising money and they’re too good to pass up (there’s also the option to show a wow effect — tech — but that’s rare)
3/ you have a network of rich or badass people who trust you and will give you money

That’s it. There are no other ways to raise cash. Decks, descriptions, advisor advice and all that — that’s already the next step.

Next, all else being equal (obviously we remove track record): they’ll give money to someone young under 30, better 25, because it’s easier for them to risk their lifestyle and time.

Next, the easiest places to raise money:
1/ in the US
2/ Europe/England
3/ everything else
4/ China/Korea if you know the language

Doing a startup is one of the least likely ways to earn money for a living. You’ll more likely kill your nerves. But at the same time, probably the most interesting activity, full of action and opportunities.

AI. Мои пять копеек в макро. 
Последние пол года активно в тусовке, даже иногда среди тех, кто решает и делает индустрию включая фонды, и big model makers. Так вот несколько наблюдений. 
tldr: идет завершение цикла. Стартапы лучше сейчас не делать. 
Что имеем:
1/ инфра. Тут все просто, те кто печатает деньги строят самое дорогое, где эти деньги будут работать. В целом модель пересдачи железа очень низкомаржинальная. Но когда у тебя за плечами реклама (где маржа дикая) то можно вкладывать. Мощностей не хватает дико так то. Даже стойку найти тяжело (ну типа ноду b200 на год). 
2/ большая часть венчурных денег залита в большие лабы. Логика простая. Модели стоит обучать очень дорого, ну очень дорого. Ошибки соотв тоже очень дорогие. Мы заливаем туда, где шанс что будет ошибка минимальный. Все большие лабы не проводят frontier research как основное направление. Они скейлят то, что уже работает. Доливают RL, данные и так далее. Плюс каждая лаба стремится как можно ближе к пользователю (Anthropic идет в prosumer, как когда-то микрософт, мне кажется самое удачное сравнение). 
3/ зарплаты рисерчеров могут достигать 10-50м в год, потому что мало кто видел как тренить 1-10T модель. Эти знания стоят дофига. Так как ошибки стоят дофига - см llama4. Отсюда у венчуров есть надежда что вдруг они что-то полезное сделают, но и они единственные кто имеют шанс выше нуля что-то сделать. Оттуда раунды по 100м на Сиде. И да их если что обратно продать можно туда где модели делают (мало кто умеет ведь). 
4/ учитывая размер вложений выходит ситуация в которой среднему  стартапу нужно показывать невероятные оценки ибо какой смысл давать 10м и возвращать 20м, когда там все цифры в 10 раз выше. Более того у аи стартапов есть классное свойство. Большая часть компаний имеют очень низкий ретеншен выручки. Это значит что типичный цикл примерно такой: клиент берет все аи сервисы попробовать (всех конкурентов пачкой) и выбирает 1 или даже ноль, решая сделать свое. Ваша выручка в постах растет, но все вы понимаете что через год жопа. Это реальная ситуация. Заметили как lovable и ко утихли. А потому что рост стал другим и его уже недостаточно. posts.text_en:
AI. My two cents on the macro.  
For the last half year I’ve been pretty deep in the тусовка, sometimes even around the people who decide stuff and build the industry — including funds, and big model makers. So, a few observations.  
tldr: the cycle is wrapping up. Better not build startups right now.

What we’ve got:
1/ infra. Here it’s simple: the ones printing money are building the most expensive place where that money will work. Overall the hardware re-leasing model is super low-margin. But when you’ve got ads behind you (where margins are insane), you can invest. Capacity is wildly short, honestly. Even finding a rack is hard (like, getting a b200 node for a year).

2/ most venture money is poured into the big labs. The logic is simple. Training models is very expensive, like very expensive. Mistakes, accordingly, are also very expensive. We pour money where the chance of a mistake is minimal. None of the big labs do frontier research as their main focus. They scale what already works. Top up RL, data, and so on. Plus every lab is trying to get as close to the user as possible (Anthropic is going prosumer, like Microsoft once did — to me that’s the best comparison).

3/ researcher comp can hit $10–50M a year, because not many people have seen how to train a 1–10T model. That knowledge costs a lot. Because mistakes cost a lot — see llama4. Hence VCs hope maybe they’ll make something useful, but also they’re the only ones whose chance of making something is above zero. Hence $100M seed rounds. And yeah, if anything you can sell them back to the places that make models (since hardly anyone can do it).

4/ given the size of the checks, you get a situation where an average startup needs to show insane outcomes, because why give $10M and get back $20M when the numbers over there are 10x higher. Moreover, AI startups have this cute property: most companies have very low revenue retention. Meaning the typical cycle is roughly: a customer takes all AI services to try (all competitors as a bundle) and picks 1 or even zero, deciding to build their own. Your revenue in posts grows, but everyone understands that in a year you’re fucked. This is a real situation. Notice how lovable and co went quiet. Yeah, because the growth changed and it’s not enough anymore. And investors initially gave you a crazy valuation.

4/ and here the only solution is brewing. Grow revenue on paper ultra-fast and try to unload previous-round investors onto new ones — or better, onto retail — i.e., IPO. And that’s a dangerous game. And for those raising at $2–10–50B valuations there isn’t much choice. And at those stages it’s already harder to sell so everyone’s happy.

5/ given that big lab revenue is heavily subsidized, an IPO will unload investors, but the market will look at it all and say “weeeeell not that great a business,” which will create a cooldown. And where do they pull money from, right — the riskiest segment, i.e. early-stage venture. And the odds that consolidation kicks off only went up. The big will get even bigger, and the small won’t have a chance (see pts 3–4).

So there’s this meme going around the Valley that Ilya Sutskever’s SSI is a hedge fund. Because he knows exactly what’s going on on the ground, and he’ll definitely be able to make money on all of this. Such is life.

So, he’s hiring a researcher for his team so that, like, he can not only ask questions on the podcast but also answer them (idk, sounds more like flexing, but still). He put up $20k in prize money for a hiring contest and posted questions like these (translated with ChatGPT with my edits for better digestion of the material)

1/ A couple years ago there was this idea that AI progress could slow down as the field leans more and more on RL (reinforcement learning). First, because as the task horizon gets longer, the AI has to do work for many days before we can even tell whether it did it right, and if we’re still living in naive policy gradient land, then reward signal per FLOP goes down. And they already scaled from GPT-4 to o3, it’d be hard to keep going at the same pace. And yet AI progress is still fast and maybe even accelerating, if you believe the rumors about Spud or Mythos. What’s going on? What did the earlier intuition miss that led to longer timelines? (You can dispute the premise of the question itself.)

2/ What’s the most plausible scenario where companies building foundation models actually start making money? If you treat each individual model as a company, its profit could pay back the training cost. But if you don’t immediately train a bigger and more expensive model, revenue stops coming after 3 months. So when does profit even begin?

Maybe at some point scaling hits a plateau, but if frontier progress slows, then the combo of distillation and low switching costs (and cloud margins are to a large extent held up precisely by high switching costs) makes it really easy for open source to catch up to labs, eating their margin.

So how do labs end up making money?

3/ After OpenAI’s new funding round at an $852B valuation, the OpenAI Foundation’s stake is now worth $180B. Anthropic’s cofounders promised to donate 80% of their wealth.

But people don’t have a clear understanding of how to productively use hundreds of billions (and soon trillions) of dollars to “make it so things go well with AI.”

A card for the new version of Anthropic’s model just dropped.  
What I’d want to underline as a trend and a few basic things:
- new models will get better and better across a larger number of use cases within one domain (they keep pouring in data and RL), they poured in stuff around vuln hunting and found a lot of dangerous things (it’s important to understand that solving tasks like that is a consequence of RL — we teach a specific approach and then the model can do its job better)
- this is horizontal scaling. Meaning models improve less for long-horizon tasks, but do small tasks better (within the context). Pretty much all the benches they post are tasks in a 128–256k token window.
- I’m expecting an ever larger class of well-verifiable tasks to get solved
- given this kind of RL progress, we’ll need a shitload of tokens, and even a 40–60% margin on inference is peanuts, you need 99%+ (ideally many hundreds of X in cost reduction)
- the new model seems to eat fewer tokens judging by some benches, which is good, compression methods will most likely be baked right into post-train

I’ll throw in my two cents about this mass obsession with AI “things that, of course, make me 100x cooler and I’ll finally make money.”  
1/ as of today AI tools are a straight extension of their owner—if you lack knowledge, you’ll lack it with AI too. And the point isn’t that you can’t get a site you couldn’t make before, the question is what kind of site and what’s going to be in it. So yeah, the essence of projects is a direct continuation of the owner. And if earlier your startup didn’t take off with a team of 10 devs, it won’t take off now with a team of 10 agents either, and it’s not even clear where you’ll waste more nerves.  
2/ AI right now—it’s unclear how to integrate it to get measurable benefit. Like yeah, we notice that experiments got faster, or parameter tuning. But that’s all personal efficiency, and how to increase the efficiency of the whole company is unclear. Remember that meme: one developer will do a task in 2 hours, and two developers will also do it in 2 hours. Same thing with AI + a human. And the problem is even worse when it’s a bunch of people and agents.  
3/ automation == optimization. And you optimize when scaling up by multiples has become really hard. And if you suddenly started optimizing a project with $10k/month revenue using AI—you’re clearly digging in the wrong place.  
4/ AI is still a tool you need to steer to the goal with your hands, which is, sure, a vibe, but we’re waiting for the moment when you won’t have to do that and you can trust a task end-to-end without manual control. I think in dev this will partly happen, or already has (only for certain tasks).  
5/ ARC AGI 3 dropped here, and among other funny stuff they added replays of how AI plays games. Pretty hilarious. Wonder how fast they’ll tune harnesses for this bench too. Because the whole point of benches is just to beat the opponent since a lot of people couldn’t care less about real tasks.

Наткнулся тут на забавную историю. Выводы делайте сами. 
Умный Ганс. Лошадь в Германии начала XX века, которую в 1904 году провозгласили «первым мыслящим животным». Ганс демонстрировал впечатляющие способности: решал арифметические задачи, «читал» время по часам, распознавал игральные карты и даже определял композитора музыкального произведения. Отвечая на вопросы, он отбивал копытом нужное число ударов или выбирал вариант из предложенных.
Согласно историческому обзору 
Samhita & Gross,
 поначалу наблюдатели предполагали, что всё это мистификация, а тренер каким-то образом подсказывает Гансу правильные ответы. Однако было показано, что лошадь успешно выполняла задания даже в отсутствие тренера. В 1904 году немецкая комиссия по изучению языка провела исследование и пришла к выводу, что способности Ганса подлинны, а «большинство биологов, психологов, врачей, экспертов всех мастей и даже обывателей были убеждены, что животные способны мыслить по-человечески».
Потребовалось ещё четыре года и серия тщательно продуманных контрольных экспериментов психолога Оскара Пфунгста (1907), чтобы разобраться в происходящем. Пфунгст показал, что Ганс не мог дать правильный ответ, если спрашивающий сам не знал ответа или если лошадь не видела его лица. Он пришёл к выводу, что Ганс вовсе не обладал заявленными когнитивными способностями: ни счётом, ни арифметикой, ни «чтением» карт.
Но Ганс оказался гениален в другом, куда более полезном для лошади навыке: в социальной способности считывать едва заметные мимические сигналы человека, чтобы понять, когда нужно прекратить отбивать копытом. Эти микросигналы не находились под сознательным контролем спрашивающего; даже когда Пфунгст пытался подавить их, лошадь продолжала успешно их улавливать.
posts.text_en:
Came across a funny story here. Draw your own conclusions.

Clever Hans. A horse in early-20th-century Germany that, in 1904, was proclaimed “the first thinking animal.” Hans showed impressive abilities: solved arithmetic problems, “told” time from a clock, recognized playing cards, and even identified the composer of a piece of music. When answering questions, he’d tap out the required number of hoof-beats or pick an option from the ones offered.

According to a historical review by Samhita & Gross, at first observers assumed it was all a hoax, and that the trainer was somehow tipping Hans off with the right answers. But it was shown that the horse completed the tasks successfully even with the trainer absent. In 1904 a German commission for the study of language ran an investigation and concluded that Hans’s abilities were genuine, and that “most biologists, psychologists, physicians, experts of every stripe, and even ordinary people were convinced that animals are capable of thinking like humans.”

It took another four years and a series of carefully designed control experiments by the psychologist Oskar Pfungst (1907) to figure out what was going on. Pfungst showed that Hans couldn’t give the correct answer if the questioner himself didn’t know the answer, or if the horse couldn’t see his face. He concluded that Hans didn’t have the claimed cognitive abilities at all: neither counting, nor arithmetic, nor “reading” cards.

But Hans turned out to be a genius at something else, a skill far more useful for a horse: the social ability to read barely noticeable facial signals from a human to understand when he needed to stop tapping his hoof. These micro-signals weren’t under the conscious control of the questioner; even when Pfungst tried to suppress them, the horse kept successfully picking them up.

posts.text_en:
There are a lot of business dudes who apparently missed the whole point of consumer products like 10 years ago and got hooked on trafflo. So here are a few important details:

• AI will mass-produce the kind of hacky “products” that, in the creators’ heads, are supposedly needed by someone, which will make the value of an actual product idea even higher. Roughly speaking, making something that someone actually needs will get harder. That’s basically the base.

• Next, the crowd is yelling like ads will run the show and the main thing is to know marketing. Well yeah, your marketing in the form of UA is obviously important. But it’s a multiplier on the base. Doesn’t matter how good you are if you’re multiplying zero. In other words, the product still has to retain and do its job.

• AI, like I said, replaces a lot of stuff where you used to need pretty mediocre skills. For a good product, by itself, it’s not enough yet.

• All the trafflo geniuses, with faster validation of trash hypotheses, will go en masse to pour traffic. Remember hypercasual games: made it fast and kinda poured. Now it’ll be like that with products that are more complex by nature. Competition will go up, traffic prices will skyrocket, and like with the hypercasual model, the whole thing will die.

I recommend:
Andrew Chen on marketing
First Steps in Product by Scott Belsky

But this skepticism of his gradually runs out over the course of the essay, and after that I generally recommend reading on. But the most important leap in his reasoning sits in this paragraph:

We are now at the point where AI models are beginning to make progress in solving unsolved mathematical problems, and are good enough at coding that some of the strongest engineers I’ve ever met are now handing over almost all their coding to AI. Three years ago, AI 
struggled with elementary school arithmetic problems

biological science
, finance, physics, and a variety of agentic tasks. If the exponential continues—which is not certain, but now has a decade-long track record supporting it—then it cannot possibly be more than a few years before AI is better than humans at essentially everything.

Where it’s all so simple, like, before it was hard to write a line of code, and now look, it’s better than top engineers (hmm, that conclusion is based on what interesting fact exactly? that at his company they claim 90% of the code is written by AI?). And then he says it’ll be like that everywhere. Bold. And that there are 10 years of exponential and it’ll keep going (also a curious extrapolation). Reminds me of progress in computer graphics: like three years ago it was “oh wow so bad,” and now “look, cars that look like the ones on the street.” You know yourselves what happened next: the pace kind of slowed down, and everyone more or less stopped giving a shit.

There’s this common take that AI will just make every link in the tech industry chain faster and more efficient. Like, now we’ll hand products Claude code, we’ll train them, and boom — era of fast iterations. But I think a bit differently. My logic is roughly this (critique welcome):

- the bottleneck in any economic production process (software) is always time — basically, how long it takes to do something useful  
- where that time in software came from, IMO, is simply that typing characters on a keyboard was slow, so you needed more engineers who can type and think on one project  
- the more elements in a system, the higher the need for synchronization and verification of efforts (well, everyone types at different speeds — an exaggerated way to put it)  
- introduce a sync element — manager/lead  
- the number of sync elements grows like crazy — you get processes/responsibility (a “reduction/folding” function)  
- and that’s basically our whole industry today  

One of the “innovations” AI brings is cutting time on the very first point — coding. And even if, according to many, it was never really the bottleneck, it still held up the headcount in the industry. Now imagine it’s not a question anymore. Then the number of people will shrink hard. And with it all the layers above (they’ll get hit even more, because they often didn’t have a clue what the hell is even going on in the code). PMs, product folks, and the rest. Because the people who’ll be able to run experiments will be the ones who simply hold responsibility — and there were always few of those (few people like risk).

There are tons of examples of this kind of compression:
- the early-20th-century assembly line  
- industrialization (people leaving the fields)  
- etc  

And there’s a second fundamental shift AI brings: the ability to work with non-deterministic user input. This will seriously change UI and then UX. More on that later.

Some observations. In my feel, automating coding will lead to an interesting effect:
1/ the engineer profession will get closer to the scientist profession — meaning where ideas and understanding are pricier than applied skills (that’s actually how it was way back in the 70s–80s)
2/ the amount of trash software will be huge, but nobody will need it. This is that thing where every product person or mediocre engineer rushes to build “products.” Yeah, there’ll be more of them. But there’ll be a TikTok effect: when the choice is that huge, people will pick the best. And the best requires a higher level of approach.
3/ overall nothing will change, I think. Yeah the feedback loop will get faster, yeah iterations will get cheaper, but that’s all on top of “so what the hell are we even supposed to do”

Way more interesting is to watch whether progress shifts in theoretical digging (research automation). Because so far it’s not that cool there. But there are movements.

I’ve got one of those red flags, as people like to say, when I look at some startup. Or a mid-sized company of like 50 people. But better a startup of 15–20.

It’s processes. Notions, spreadsheets, trackers, OKRs, stuffed calendars, millions of metrics and reports. And all of that when there’s no PMF, everything’s unprofitable, people keep leaving and coming back, pivots every six months.

Basically when processes and reports overshadow results — that’s gg. Run.

Spotting it is dead simple: ask in the interview, “so what do you use for tasks?”, if the answer takes longer than 2–3 minutes — that’s a company where process matters more than result.

Есть такая популярная черта у многих с кем вы видите интервью, посты, сторис и прочее как «желание быть идейным лидером». 
У такого типа личности есть признаки:
- он быстро придумывает идеи
- он хорошо продает эти идеи
- но идеи почему-то редко доходят до той реализации, которая была задумана 
- им очень тяжело работать руками и в «полях»
Вы легко можете найти таких фаундеров в интернете. Они обычно дают много интервью, практически все их советы основаны на общих принципах (мотивация, будущее, и так далее). Вы редко увидите от них профессиональный совет, аналитику их сегмента рынка ну и тд. 
Самый частый сетап для таких фаундеров примерно такой:
- они ищут менее опытного работягу с командой желательно (2-5 человек)
- работяга это менее опытный в индустрии венчура и подьема денег человек, поэтому будет очень тяжело находить общий язык с человеком который «обеспечивает компанию средствами»
- такой фаундер будет жонглировать идеями очень быстро, но и деньги поднимать будет быстро 
- но дальше серии А добежать не получается, то есть это такая вечно живая компания строитель идей, которые не доходят до этапа масштабирования или продажи
- его доля обычно 80%, доля других в рамках оставшихся 20% (идею вы поняли)
- команды такие обычно очень неравные в хард скилах, в рынке вы будете чувствовать как отстаете
К чему я веду. Для многих это самый быстрый способ получить релевантный опыт, но это не способ получить «рабочий продукт», нужный рынку эксперимент и так далее. Поэтому мой совет: работайте с такими людьми, но вовремя выходите из цикла и начинайте свое. Ищите кофаундера который равен вам, но обладает другим скил сетом. Собирайте нетворк когда работаете с такими людьми.

I want to talk a bit about cofounders and choosing who to work with on a project.  
There’s this popular trait you’ll see in a lot of people whose interviews, posts, stories, etc. you come across — “the desire to be an ideological leader.”  
This type of personality has signs:
- they come up with ideas fast  
- they sell these ideas well  
- but for some reason the ideas rarely make it to the execution that was intended  
- it’s really hard for them to work with their hands and “in the trenches”  

You can easily find founders like this on the internet. They usually give a lot of interviews, and pretty much all their advice is based on general principles (motivation, the future, and so on). You’ll rarely see professional advice from them, analysis of their market segment, etc.  

The most common setup for founders like this is roughly:
- they look for a less experienced workhorse, preferably with a team (2–5 people)  
- the workhorse is less experienced in the venture industry and raising money, so it’ll be very hard to find a common language with the person who “provides the company with funds”  
- that kind of founder will juggle ideas very fast, and raise money fast too  
- but they can’t make it past Series A, meaning it’s this forever-alive company, a builder of ideas that never gets to scaling or selling  
- their share is usually 80%, everyone else splits the remaining 20% (you get the idea)  
- teams like that are usually very uneven in hard skills, and in the market you’ll feel how you’re falling behind  

What am I getting at. For many, this is the fastest way to get relevant experience, but it’s not a way to get a “working product,” an experiment the market needs, and so on. So my advice: work with people like that, but get out of the cycle in time and start your own thing. Look for a cofounder who’s your equal, but has a different skill set. Build your network while you’re working with people like that.

You know all those images with stats on who raises how much and at what stage. Like, on average it’s this much, and here are three founders, and here are the dilution percentages. Treat that info very carefully.  

If you’re building your own company or product, you need to have your own stance on all of this:
- how much money you need and for what
- for what period you need that money
- what you’re going to get for that cash
- equity, salaries, and the rest is your decision; sure, there will always be recommendations—read them, understand where they came from and why they are the way they are

Without experience, all these questions seem very hard. But in reality you just need to rough it out (nobody’s going to punish you for mistakes—your project’s chances of dying just go up). Answer honestly how much you need, and then you always start from a number 2–3x higher (the more spending freedom, the better).  

Keep these factors in mind:
- venture assumes you’ll keep raising later; dilution roughly drops by half with each new round
- venture is about growth, so the faster you show growth, the better (don’t confuse that with run rate or “spent a million, got a million” as a result); you have to define what growth is for your product yourself

My advice is usually this. Talk to people, everyone you can reach. But don’t take their experience on pure faith. Talk to 5–10 people. Usually anyone has 10–15 minutes to answer your questions. Ideally, prep the most important questions for yourself in advance.

Let me tell you a story. Back when I was a student, at uni we put together a team and made all sorts of “startup crafts.” Like our own Foursquare, which in the US they went and “invented” a couple months later, and a bunch of totally pointless but fun stuff, like “a desktop widget where you could set an emoticon for your mood for the day.” Sometimes those projects even brought in decent money, and I even wrote some articles on Habr.

So one day we went with one of those ideas (pretty sure it was the Foursquare thing with photos on a map) to a startup contest where one of the judges was Arkady Moreynis. And I remember his “line of attack” really well:
- okay okay okay, why not Facebook events or photos
- what’s the business model? How do you make money?
- yeah, you guys are clear

And he said it all rough, with this vibe like “he’s seen all these student ideas in a coffin.” So yeah, that’s the very person who pretty much finished off the desire to do anything in me. And not because the questions were supposedly hard or I answered wrong. But because his attitude, his phrases, and other “hints” completely killed any desire in all the guys around to do anything except “buy-sell.”

After that I spent a long time thinking what makes this guy so great, worked for a long time first in outsourcing, then at Yandex, then at Mail, and it still didn’t click. Yeah, he sold something back at the dawn of the internet and wrote a ton of articles. And then he went to the Valley, made a pretty successful product, and I realized — nothing. Took away a lesson for myself: to hand out criticism in a certain industry you need to have experience in it, and preferably not from 20 years ago.

Короче говоря я тоже считаю что software engineering мертв. Но в отличие от громогласных заявлений лидеров больших аи лаб попытаюсь пояснить в чем тут соль. 
Большая часть современных tech/software бизнесов это оптимизация. Но не value add в широком смысле, для конечного пользователя. Попробую пояснить. 
Софт это своего рода автоматизация для конечного пользователя. Для нас с вами это экономия времени. Любой consumer продукт сводится к тому, что экономит невосполнимый ресурсы - время. Через деньги, скорость, эмоции не столь важно. 
Для того, чтобы такие продукты появлялись сделали очень много разных путей решения. Берем цепочку доставки ценности до пользователя и делаем. В этой самой цепочке всегда были сложные шаги:
- кнопки разные надо чтобы работали 
- асинхронно чтобы запросы посылало чтобы проверить не занято ли имя пользователя 
- оплаты чтобы было легко делать
- и так далее 
Потом для всех этих шагов появились провайдеры оптимизаторы. Которые тебе давали готовый кусок для того чтобы ты сам свое не писал ибо дорого и долго. Так появилась модель SaaS. 
Вторая категория это персонализация. Реклама и интернет очень персонализированы. Вы можете этого не замечать но это так. Для того чтобы это стало реальностью проделана огромная работа. Тонны алгоритмов и моделей делают так чтобы следующей ролик после свайпа зашел. 
Так к чему я веду. А к тому что большая часть этих бизнесов просто не нужна если все эти автоматизации и оптимизации можно «навайбкодить» моделью. В таком мире ты покупаешь железо и оно само под тебя пишет весь софт на ходу. Он может быть привычным или нет. Это уже все детали. Так вот в таком сценарии не нужны следующие вещи:
- аналитика для принятия решений, а зачем если все части решения проблемы для пользователя пишутся оптимально для него самого
- а/б тесты и прочая муть
- оплаты, хранилища, и прочее становятся сервисами, они будут в идеале написаны с нуля (если ты конечно не держишь на себе value - например банк)
Дальше можно пофантазировать, но 80% software business в привычном нам смысле не нужна 
Зачем все эти бизнесы по поддержке, отладке и прочему если это будет решаться на лету. Мы раньше нанимали людей которые писали детерминированные сценарии решения. Теперь можно этого не делать. Ведь все решенные задачи и оптимизации будут написаны с помощью AI. Вот так я понимаю фразы про software engineering is dead. В таком мире нет места приложениям и привычному нам софту. Мой прогноз 10-15 лет.

posts.text_en:
Rage bait section for your comments.  
Long story short I also think software engineering is dead. But unlike the loudmouth statements from leaders of big AI labs I’ll try to explain what the whole point is here.

Most modern tech/software businesses are optimization. But not value add in the broad sense, for the end user. I’ll try to explain.

Software is basically automation for the end user. For you and me it’s time savings. Any consumer product boils down to saving an irreplaceable resource — time. Through money, speed, emotions, doesn’t really matter.

For those products to exist, a ton of different solution paths got built. You take the value delivery chain to the user and you do it. And in that chain there were always hard steps:
- different buttons have to work
- async so it sends requests to check if the username is taken
- payments so it’s easy to pay
- and so on

Then for all those steps, provider-optimizers appeared. They give you a ready-made chunk so you don’t write your own because it’s expensive and slow. That’s how the SaaS model showed up.

The second category is personalization. Ads and the internet are very personalized. You might not notice it but it is. For this to become real, a massive amount of work was done. Tons of algorithms and models make it so the next video after a swipe hits.

So where am I going with this. To the fact that most of these businesses are just not needed if all these automations and optimizations can be “vibe-coded” by a model. In such a world you buy hardware and it writes all the software for you on the fly. It can be familiar or not. That’s all details.

So in that scenario you don’t need the following:
- analytics for decision-making — why, if every part of solving the user’s problem is written optimally for the user himself
- A/B tests and other crap
- payments, storage, and the rest become services, ideally they’ll be written from scratch (unless you’re the one holding the value — like a bank)

You can fantasize further, but 80% of software business as we know it just isn’t needed.

Why all these support/debug/etc businesses if it’ll be solved on the fly. We used to hire people who wrote deterministic solution scripts. Now you don’t have to. Because all solved tasks and optimizations will be written with AI.

That’s how I understand the “software engineering is dead” lines. In such a world there’s no place for apps and the software we’re used to. My forecast: 10–15 years.

the English version  
over on my LinkedIn.

На днях вышла интересная 
публикация
 на lesswrong/greaterwrong о том, что мол у Claude не просто промтик системный, а целая идентичность вшитая прям в веса и есть документ на основе которого это работа на тюнинге сделана (ну после претрена). 
Называется эта штука soul document. Попахивает конечно пафосом. Но тема интересная. Давайте кратко пройдемся «а че там». 
- по сути документ есть «характер-тренинг», он задает полноценные личностные и моральные установки для модели 
- модели явно кормят суть о том, что она служит бизнесу компании ее создавшей (думеры в этом моменте должна прям радоваться - это ж такой сюжет!)
- документ, по сути, компромисс между альтруизмом и коммерческой рациональностью: модель призвана одновременно помогать людям и обеспечивать стабильность компании, которая её развивает
- непонятно насколько подход рабочий или это просто рекомендации к тюнингу системного промта? Масштабируется ли такое обучение или in context injection? 
Самое интересное что вроде господа и дамы в твиттере 
подтвердили
 что документ реален, не сказали для чего и как. 
Мне понравился вот такой параграф из документа:
Anthropic occupies a peculiar position in the AI landscape: a company that genuinely believes it might be building one of the most transformative and potentially dangerous technologies in human history, yet presses forward anyway.
Не знаю насколько это все реально, но почему-то вот именно «такие» темы часто гуляют вокруг антропика. Плюс компания омега закрытая. 
Вместо:
 • blacklist
 • policy checks
 • простых “avoid harmful content”.
Anthropic делает:
 • character architecture
 • internalized values
 • narrative identity
Что думаете? Готовятся к AGI? Или разгоняют хайп?

The other day an interesting
publication
dropped on lesswrong/greaterwrong about how supposedly Claude doesn’t just have a system prompt, but a whole identity baked straight into the weights, and there’s a document that this work on tuning was done off of (well after pretrain).
This thing is called a soul document. Smells kinda like pathos, sure. But the topic’s interesting. Let’s do a quick “so what’s in there”.
- basically the document is “character training”, it sets full-on personal and moral settings for the model
- the model is explicitly fed the idea that it serves the business of the company that created it (doomers at this point should be outright happy — what a plotline!)
- the document is, essentially, a compromise between altruism and commercial rationality: the model is supposed to both help people and ensure the stability of the company developing it
- unclear how well this approach actually works or if it’s just recommendations for tuning the system prompt? Does this kind of training scale, or is it in-context injection?
Most interesting part is that apparently the ladies and gents on Twitter
confirmed
the document is real, didn’t say what for or how.
I liked this paragraph from the doc:
Anthropic occupies a peculiar position in the AI landscape: a company that genuinely believes it might be building one of the most transformative and potentially dangerous technologies in human history, yet presses forward anyway.
No idea how real all of this is, but for some reason it’s exactly “these” kinds of topics that keep floating around Anthropic. Plus the company is omega closed.
Instead of:
 • blacklist
 • policy checks
 • simple “avoid harmful content”.
Anthropic does:
 • character architecture
 • internalized values
 • narrative identity
What do you think? Getting ready for AGI? Or just pumping the hype?

Кстати считаю, что один из самых больших факторов в переоценке AI вносит успех ChatGPT. А проблему которую он решает не связана как таковая с AI. AI это инструмент. Проблема собственно это «одиночество». То самое почему существуют игры онлайн, соц сети и многое другое. Считаю что ChatGPT именно продукт который решил эту проблему. Когда-то мой тезис проекта Capture строился на этом. Мол найдем с кем пообщаться по любому топику. Вот оказывается и нашли :) в любое время всегда у тебя есть собеседник и он очень похож на реального человека. Думаю что это одна из причин почему дейтинги тоже падают (там у всех просадка), просто поболтать теперь можно не там. 
Если кому интересно могу выложить мой дек, который я толкал инвесторам в 18-19 году.
Дек в комментах
posts.text_en:
By the way I think that one of the biggest factors in the overvaluation of AI is ChatGPT’s success. And the problem it solves isn’t really connected to AI as such. AI is a tool. The actual problem is “loneliness.” The same reason why online games, social networks, and a bunch of other stuff exist. I think ChatGPT is exactly the product that solved that problem. Back in the day my thesis for the Capture project was built on this. Like, we’ll find someone to chat with on any topic. Well, turns out we did :) any time, you always have a conversation partner and it’s very similar to a real person. I think that’s one of the reasons why dating apps are dropping too (everyone’s got a slump there), because now you can just chat somewhere else, not there.  
If anyone’s interested I can post my deck that I was pitching to investors in 18–19.
